sources.entry: Hitting the High Notes - Joel Spolsky

summary.title: Hitting the High Notes
summary.one_liner: Joe Spolsky argues that top programmers matter because their productivity varies several-fold and great software comes from talent that mediocre teams cannot reach, using Yale student timing data and product examples.
keywords: design adds value faster than cost
takeaways: Programmer productivity differences in a controlled class assignment dataset were roughly 3x to 10x between fastest and slowest students.
Time spent was uncorrelated with grade quality among top-quartile students, per the author's analysis of the Yale data.
Adding more mediocre programmers does not substitute for a few great ones, due to coordination overhead (Brooks' Law) and lack of top-end quality.
Because software duplication is free, spending on good programmers is spread over every copy sold, so skimping on programmers rarely saves much.
In winner-take-all software markets, a product must be remarkably good, so hiring top talent is presented as the key lever.
summary.summary: This is a 2005 essay by Joel Spolsky, written as part of his series on building a software company. He argues that the 'best programmers' premise holds by analysing timing data from a Yale programming course, where hours spent varied widely among students with objective, test-based grades. He then argues that mediocre teams cannot reach the 'high notes' of great software, illustrating with examples such as Winamp, the iPod, and Windows Media Player. The piece is persuasive and anecdotal rather than a how-to, and the data analysis is acknowledged as imperfect.
